newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish T-bill yields seen rising on low demand.
newsitem.headline: Polish T-bill yields seen rising on low demand.

text.p: Polish T-bill yields are expected to rise again at next week's tender amid low demand after the central bank warned that it might tighten monetary policy further to curb the country's robust domestic demand, dealers said.
Foreign investors were expected to remain sidelined at Monday's 1.1 billion zloty tender amid concern about the currency and the outcome of parliamentary polls due on September 21.

"Foreigners may enter in small amounts, but generally they are waiting for the elections and the market should remain sleepy unless the central bank makes a move," said Piotr Bednarek, senior T-bill dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

The National Bank of Poland (NBP) had said that it may tighten the monetary screws once again after upping rates in early August since commercial banks had not raised credit and deposit rates sufficiently after the official rate increase.

The NBP signalled that it may use other instruments in its portfolio to put the brakes on credit growth, such as increasing obligatory reserve levels, creating credit caps for commercial banks or opening deposit accounts for the public.

Dealers said that the yield of the benchmark 52-week T-bill should be capped around 22.90 percent on Monday against this week's average yield of 22.63 percent, and that investor focus will remain on the shorter eight and 13-week paper.

"The 22.90 percent level should be the upper barrier for the longer papers on Monday and the upward trend is likely to continue until foreign investors return to Polish paper," said Marcin Dec, dealer at Bank Gdanski SA.
The central bank's sabre-rattling boosted the zloty to its one-month high against the currency basket before a NBP currency-buying intervention pushed it back early in the week.
Dealers said the zloty should remain locked around one percent weaker than parity next week, but added that if it did break out of its corridor it would be on the downside.
The zloty is traded within a 14 percent band around a central parity rate, which is set by the NBP daily against a basket of currencies.

"It may hold around one percent or slowly weaken as the country's current account gap is growing and foreigners are not showing much interest in Poland," said Mateusz Bieniek, forex dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw.
Dealers said that even if the zloty continued to drift slowly in either direction it was unlikely to trigger NBP interventions.

"The NBP probably wants the zloty to be weak, but it doesn't want the currency to weaken quickly...so it is not clear whether the central bank will be waiting at minus 1.5 percent if the zloty slowly fell to that level," Bieniek said.
The NBP has previously supported the zloty at minus 1.5 percent.
The zloty ended the week at 3.4870 to the dollar and at 1.9000 to the mark, or 1.07 percent weaker than parity against last week's close at minus 0.74 percent.
Dealers said that next week one-day rates on the money market should continue to drift slightly below the NBP's new benchmark 14-day reverse repo level of 23.55 percent.
But they said rates may briefly rise as liquidity dropped during monthly tax payments around August 20.
